attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: Keeps the universal 'every time', both limbs, and 'seem'. Context points to OpenAI and Anthropic. 'Seem' reports an impression of a pattern; it is not a probability hedge.

contract.note: Reading 'lower/higher' as against earlier expectations for the same period is an ordinary reading of the speaker's firm universal wording. Calendar 2025 is an inferred period. One clear exception on the revenue limb is enough to contradict 'every time'.

evidence.note: CNBC, citing unnamed sources, reports OpenAI's realized 2025 revenue at $13.1B against a $10B target. This is a same-company, same-period exception to the revenue limb. The cash-burn figure does not test total costs.

reviews.rationale: The claim says that every report shows lower revenue. OpenAI's 2025 revenue, as reported, beat its earlier target by about $3B, which contradicts that universal on the revenue limb. The cost limb is not tested, because cash burn is not total expenses. The source is an attributed estimate, which the contract admits.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The 'software companies' scope fits the context ('[Software company] is still growing'). 'Much' has no threshold.

contract.note: The plain reading (AI's share of recognized revenue and growth at established software vendors) is ordinary and fair. The materiality threshold and the population are evaluator choices.

evidence.note: Salesforce company disclosure of $800M Agentforce ARR. This is ARR, not recognized AI revenue, and comes from one company. It is listed as counterevidence but does not settle the claim.
Workday's count of AI actions is a usage metric. It gives no measure of AI revenue.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only ARR and usage metrics from two companies. There is no comparable recognized AI revenue against total revenue across a representative set, so the claim can be neither supported nor contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The speaker never says '$30B of funding' or 'lifetime revenue'. The $30B most plausibly refers to the single Series G round, or is loose shorthand. 'Bad business' is a normative judgment. The line works as rhetorical shorthand, not a measured comparison.

contract.note: Reading $30B as cumulative funding comes from the drafter, not the speaker, and it alone drives the contradiction. The packet itself identifies $30B as a single round. This stretches the words against the speaker.

evidence.note: The CFO declaration gives revenue over $5B (consistent with the $5B) and over $60B raised in total. The $60B contradicts only the contract's cumulative-funding reading, which the speaker did not supply.

reviews.rationale: The '$30B into $5B' line is ambiguous rhetorical shorthand with a normative conclusion attached. The contradiction depends entirely on reading $30B as cumulative funding, which the speaker did not supply. On a fair reading the $5B revenue matches the filing and the $30B referent cannot be scored.

semantics.note: This isolates the OpenAI affordability aside. 'Cannot afford' may look forward to future Oracle payments rather than past ones.

contract.note: The liquidity reading is ordinary. Choosing Q4 2025 is an evaluator decision, and it may miss the speaker's forward-looking sense, since most of the payments for these data centers fall later. That choice could decide the result.

evidence.note: Attributed annual cash-burn figure. It does not match Oracle payments or quarter-level liquidity.

OpenAI company disclosure announcing $110B of new investment, dated Feb 2026, outside the target quarter. It does not show cash received or Oracle bills covered. Listed as counterevidence but only context.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no Oracle payment schedule and no matched unrestricted cash or available financing for the target period. The cash-burn and funding-announcement items are context only, so OpenAI's ability to pay remains unsettled.
